transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Laura (Keystone Head of Data), Tom (Keystone Platform), Amir (Keystone Security), Sofia (Keystone Product)
Recording id: rec-ff-20270418-0892

Summary: quick alignment on success criteria; detailed workload numbers requested; plan benchmarks and share security pack

00:00 Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, I'm Maya, AE for Redwood Inference, with Diego our SE. Quick intros?
00:18 Laura (Keystone): Hey Maya, Laura here, Head of Data. Our goal is to evaluate LLMs for transaction summarization and in-line customer message routing.
00:28 Diego (Redwood): Great, can you frame the expected traffic and success metrics so we can size the POC?
00:35 Tom (Keystone): Sure — current peak is around 120 rps during batch windows, average around 30 rps. But our concurrency is spiky; we see bursts up to ~140 QPS for ~10-12 minutes.
00:48 Maya (Redwood): When you say rps, that's requests per second inbound, right? And typical request size?
00:55 Tom: Yes inbound requests. Token-wise it's mixed — about 70% short queries under 200 input tokens, 20% medium 200-800, and 10% long requests where customers attach full conversation transcripts up to 2k tokens. Output tokens usually smaller — median 50-80 tokens, 95th around 400.
01:14 Diego: Ok that's helpful. For modeling we'll need a sample of request logs (timestamps, input token counts, output token counts) so we can recreate real QPS/concurrency and simulate batching and KV cache behavior.
01:26 Laura: We'll extract logs, but need to make sure they're redacted. We can provide sanitized headers and token counts no PII.
01:33 Amir (Keystone): From a security perspective we're leaning toward a Private deployment or Dedicated with strict VPC and KMS; we handle sensitive transaction metadata. We require SOC2, SSO (SAML), and audit logs.
01:46 Maya: Totally expected for finance. We have Redwood Private options — private control plane with customer-managed networking. We'll include SOC2 + ISO paperwork. Also support KMS/HSM integrations.
01:54 Sofia: Timeline? We'd like a 6 week POC and decision by the end of May.
02:01 Maya: Reasonable. Typical POC is 4-8 weeks. Key success criteria we'll propose: meet throughput targets (peak and sustained), latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99), and quality thresholds for summaries/classification compared to your baseline.
02:12 Tom: For latency, we want p95 under 300ms for short requests and p99 under 600ms overall. Is that realistic?
02:21 Diego: For short requests on optimized hosting and batching it's achievable. p99 depends on queuing and KV cache hit rates — with dedicated capacity and quantized model variants we can hit those numbers for majority of traffic. For long context requests p99 will be higher — we'll model those separately.
02:40 Laura: We also care about cost per token. We'll want tradeoffs: quantized models vs latency and potential quality drop.
02:48 Maya: Right, Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles — 8-bit or 4-bit QAT style, and we'd measure quality regressions on your eval set.
02:56 Diego: For the POC benchmark plan: we suggest 1) you provide 7 days of sample logs with token counts and QPS profile, 2) Redwood will run baseline on a hosted config then on a Dedicated pool, 3) measure p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1M tokens, 4) run a handful of eval prompts for quality metrics.
03:18 Laura: Sounds good. Can we split tests by request class? e.g., short (<200), medium (200-800), long (>800)?
03:25 Diego: Absolutely, we'll run stratified traffic to match your distribution. Also we'll include a KV cache experiment to show prefix caching benefits on conversational sessions.
03:35 Tom: For concurrency, we ramp to peak in 10 minutes and sustain 120 QPS for a 15 minute window. Expect burstiness.
03:44 Diego: We'll reproduce bursts and test autoscaling/burst capacity. For Dedicated you can reserve baseline capacity and allow burst to shared pools.
03:53 Amir: Audit trail is non-negotiable. We need per-request logs and token-level cost breakdown for compliance.
04:00 Maya: We can provide token-level usage and trace links. We also support retention controls and log export to your SIEM.
04:08 Laura: On model selection: we plan to start with an open model like Mistral or Llama variant, possibly try an instruction-tuned model. We may also test a smaller embedding model for routing.
04:19 Diego: We'll include a model matrix. For heavy throughput, smaller instruction-tuned models with quantization will reduce cost; we can also test hybrid routing — short queries to smaller model, long context to larger model.
04:35 Sofia: Quality bar: for summarization we want human raters to prefer Redwood outputs to our baseline 70% of the time. For classification > 92% accuracy.
04:45 Maya: We'll operationalize that into the POC eval harness — share the eval prompts and expected labels.
04:51 Tom: About private deployment — we have a VPC in AWS eu-west-1 and a policy that keys must stay in regional KMS. Can Redwood support regional KMS and a private control plane?
05:03 Maya: Yes. Our Private option supports regional KMS and customer-managed network peering. We'll share the architecture doc.
05:10 Amir: Encryption at rest and in transit, HSM for key wrapping, and audit logs streaming to our SIEM.
05:17 Diego: Noted. We'll attach a security checklist and a sample network diagram.
05:23 Laura: Ok, on benchmarks can you give an initial estimate of GPU footprint for peak? 120 QPS with mixed tokens?
05:31 Diego: Rough back-of-envelope: if majority are short (~<200 tokens) and outputs short, one A100-class instance can handle roughly 80-150 short completions depending on batching and context. For your mix with 10% long context we'll propose a 2-3 GPU Dedicated pool for baseline, with autoscale to 4 for sustained burst windows. We'll provide precise model-kernel sizing after we ingest logs.
05:55 Maya: We'll include a capacity plan doc with cost estimates.
06:02 Laura: For acceptance criteria, recap: 1) reproduce your traffic pattern in Redwood benchmark, 2) meet p95/p99 targets for short/medium requests, 3) cost per 1M tokens within our target, 4) quality thresholds met on eval set, 5) security checklist satisfied.
06:22 Maya: Correct. We'll translate into a formal SOW.
06:27 Tom: Any blockers on our side? We need to prepare sanitized logs and open a time-limited S3 bucket or secure upload for Redwood to pull artifacts.
06:36 Maya: We'll send secure upload instructions and a sample logs schema.
06:41 Diego: Also a note on KV cache: if your workload has many repeated prefixes, you can get 20-40% token savings. Send a sample session grouping.
06:51 Laura: We'll try to extract sessions and token patterns.
06:56 Amir: Regarding compliance, we'll need a list of sub-processors and their locations.
07:02 Maya: We'll attach sub-processor list and data flow diagrams.
07:07 Sofia: Last question: how do you measure hallucination/regression during the POC?
07:13 Diego: We'll run targeted eval sets and human-in-the-loop review. For classification we'll use labeled holdouts; for summarization a small human rater panel to validate quality.
07:23 Laura: OK, that's helpful.
07:28 Maya: Great — let's recap next steps. We'll send SOW and security pack by 2027-04-20, you provide logs by 2027-04-19, Diego will run baseline benchmarks by 2027-04-25, and we'll sync after the first run.
07:44 Tom: Works for us. Thanks.
07:48 Maya: Thanks everyone, I'll follow up in calendar and email.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., Redwood Dedicate, K-V cash), some filler words, and speaker interruptions retained.
questions: Can Redwood support regional KMS and a private control plane?
What are realistic p95/p99 targets for mixed token workloads?
How will quantization affect quality for our summarization use case?
